questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman was reviewed on the ward due to nausea and several diarrheal stools. She had recently sustained a cerebrovascular accident. She had no known drug allergies. Investigations: Total white cell count 22,000/mm3 Serum creatinine 2.5 mg/dL Normal liver function tests Blood and urine cultures were positive for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, sensitivities pending
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ceftazidime IV Aztreonam is best reserved for treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in patients with severe beta-lactam allergy. The patient is not a candidate for oral antibiotic therapy due to recent gastrointestinal disturbances. The patient is also elderly, has renal insufficiency, and has experienced recent central nervous system pathology, each of which increases risk for carbapenem-induced seizures. Aminoglycoside therapy would be risky given the patient’s renal function and is not preferred for monotherapy of serious Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections. Ceftazidime is a first-line therapy for treatment of Pseudomonas infections.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q5

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of fevers. She had AML for which she was on induction chemotherapy. She had a tunneled intravenous catheter. On examination, there were no signs of infection around her CVC site. There were two necrotic skin lesions on her right lower leg. Investigations: Neutrophil count 0.1 ×109/L Blood and wound cultures grew gram-negative bacilli
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa Pseudomonas infections are commonly considered as important causes of neutropenic fever. This patient presented also with skin lesions, which could be consistent with ecthyma gangrenosum, of which Pseudomonas is an important cause. The other gram-negative bacteria listed can certainly cause BSI but would be less likely in this scenario.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q15

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman was diagnosed with healthcareassociated pneumonia. She was a nursing home resident with no drug allergies, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and acute on chronic kidney disease. Investigations: Creatinine clearance 25 mL/min (baseline creatinine clearance 40 mL/min) Sputum culture negative Multiplex PCR respiratory virus panel negative
questions.lead_in: What antipseudomonal agent poses the greatest risk for neurotoxicity?
questions.explanation: Cefepime While each of the beta-lactam antibiotics listed has the potential to cause neurotoxicity, cefepime is most associated with the development of this adverse effect. A US Food and Drug Administration safety alert for cefepime identified age >50 and inadequate renal dosing adjustments as risk factors for neurotoxicity.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q4

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient admitted with STEMI, now status-post CABG, and with a complicated hospital course thereafter, including prolonged respiratory failure requiring tracheostomy and gastrostomy tube placements, who also received several days of broad-spectrum antibiotics postoperatively because of shock, and concern for possible sepsis, is now having increasing supplemental oxygen requirement and fever. His chest radiograph shows diffuse pulmonary opacities, worst in the right-lower lobe. His nurse also has noted increasingly profuse and purulent tracheal secretions. He was started on linezolid and meropenem, but after 2 days he was still having fevers, and his respiratory status continued to worsen. Tracheal aspirate culture is now growing an organism that was identified as an oxidase-positive, nonfermenting gram-negative bacillus.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia This patient has hospital-acquired pneumonia and did not demonstrate clinical improvement on broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy. He has multiple risk factors for development of drug-resistant pathogens, including his prolonged ICU stay and antecedent antibiotic therapy. Linezolid and meropenem would provide more than adequate activity against most gram-positive and gram-negative pathogens, including those that would produce extended-spectrum β-lactamases. Stenotrophomonas can be a cause of HAP , is intrinsically resistant to the antibiotic agents that he has been receiving, and is a nonfermenting gram-negative bacillus that is oxidase-positive. Other nonfermenting, oxidase-positive gram-negative bacilli include Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Achromobacter, and Burkholderia, among others.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q31

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with 4 days of mildly pruritic rash, predominantly around his groin, and on his legs. He was otherwise feeling well. On exam, he was noted to have multiple punctate areas of erythema, surrounding hair follicles in his groin and on both legs. He had no palmoplantar lesions. He also mentioned that he had spent several hours in his hot tub the week before he noticed the rash.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his folliculitis?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa This patient likely has hot tub folliculitis, which is most commonly caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa . This infection is usually self-limited and does not require systemic antibiotic therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q30

questions.stem: A 30-year-old firefighter sustained third-degree burns to his forearms and hands. He was admitted to the burn unit and underwent wound debridement that evening. The next day, he developed significant erythema and induration involving his burn wounds.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus Gram-positive bacteria ( Staphylococcus, Streptococcus) are the most common organisms associated with burn wound infections immediately following injury. The shift to gramnegative bacteria (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa , Acinetobacter spp.) and fungi occurs several days later, particularly with prolonged hospitalization and broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q28

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man presented with fever and a new skin lesion. He was known to have had a prolonged neutropenia for at least 28 days following chemotherapy. He had a tunnelled line in situ which had been placed 10 days earlier. On examination, his temperature was 38.7°C. He had an erythematous lesion with central necrosis on his left leg. It was nontender.
questions.lead_in: What organism is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa This is a picture typical of ecthyma gangrenosum. Ecthyma gangrenosum is classically associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia in the setting of immunocompromise. It can also (but less commonly) develop with Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Candida albicans among others, especially gram-negatives. It is usually due to hematogenous dissemination of the pathogen, with subsequent invasion of small vessel walls, leading to ischemia and necrosis distally. Typically lesions start as painless macules which evolve rapidly into indurated bullae which then become necrotic. Multiple molds can invade the vascular endothelium causing necrotic skin lesions as well as systemic involvement, such as Aspergillus, Fusarium, and Mucor. In the setting of neutropenia and necrotic skin lesions, additional imaging seeking thoracic and abdominal lesions due to angioinvasive molds would also be appropriate.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q49

questions.question: Name the most likely mechanism of resistance for each isolate.
questions.question_raw: Name the most likely mechanism of resistance

parts.text: Serratia marcescens resistant to ertapenem, imipenem AND meropenem, but susceptible to ceftriaxone.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to meropenem, but susceptible to imipenem.
Staphylococcus aureus resistant to daptomycin.
Enterococcus gallinarum resistant to vancomycin, but susceptible to teicoplanin.
Enterobacter cloacae intermediate to ertapenem, but susceptible to meropenem and cefepime.

parts_raw.text: Serratia marcescens resistant to ertapenem, imipenem AND meropenem, but susceptible to Ceftriaxone
Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to Meropenem, but susceptible to Imipenem
Staphylococcus aureus resistant to daptomycin
Enterococcus gallinarum resistant to vancomycin, but susceptible to teicoplanin
Enterobacter cloacae intermediate to ertapenem, but susceptible to meropenem and cefepime

questions.model_answer: a) Class A carbapenemase (enzymatic inactivation), e.g., chromosomal SME (or OXA-48-type), which hydrolyzes carbapenems while sparing extended-spectrum cephalosporins. b) Upregulated efflux (MexAB-OprM) - meropenem is a substrate but imipenem is not; imipenem resistance would instead require OprD porin loss. c) Cell-membrane target alteration (increased net positive surface charge, e.g., mprF), reducing binding of calcium-dependent daptomycin. d) VanC ligase producing D-Ala-D-Ser termini - intrinsic, low-level vancomycin resistance in E. gallinarum with retained teicoplanin susceptibility. e) Derepression/hyperexpression of chromosomal AmpC combined with porin (permeability) loss.
questions.beyond_mandell: Detailed resistance mechanisms are covered in Mandell Ch. 18 (antimicrobial resistance), not this organism chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Carbapenemase (enzyme inactivation) by SME (oxa-48 also can show this pattern). Pseudomonas: RND efflux pump MexAB-OprM (meropenem/doripenem, but not imipenem, are substrates of this efflux system). S. aureus/dapto: Target-site alteration (change in bacterial cell membrane composition) - dapto requires calcium to become positively charged and interacts with negatively charged lipid moieties on membrane to kill; increased positive charge on membrane prevents dapto action. E. gallinarum: Target-site alteration - VanC (specific to E. gallinarum); vancomycin binds terminal D-ala-D-ala residues of growing PG cell wall; VanA isolates show high MICs to Vancomycin and Teicoplanin, VanB/VanC often have lower MICs to Vancomycin and are S to Teicoplanin. Enterobacter cloacae: Hyperexpression of ampC + porin change combination.

questions.question: Ceftolozane-tazobactam in multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

parts.text: Name three resistance mechanisms that it can overcome.

parts_raw.text: Ceftolozane-tazobactam in MDR pseudomonas. Name three resistance mechanisms that it can overcome.

questions.model_answer: (1) Loss/decreased expression of the OprD outer-membrane porin (carbapenem-selective permeability defect). (2) Upregulation of RND efflux pumps (MexAB-OprM, MexXY-OprM). (3) AmpC chromosomal cephalosporinase (enhanced PBP affinity keeps it active). Ceftolozane-tazobactam has enhanced affinity for P. aeruginosa PBPs and is unaffected by porin loss or efflux upregulation, so >80% of ceftazidime- or meropenem-resistant isolates remain susceptible; it does NOT overcome metallo-β-lactamases or KPC.

cohort_answer.text: Overexpression of efflux pumps; Loss of the outer membrane porin OprD; Not affected by beta lactamases both AmpC and ESBLs; Overcomes modification of PBPs

questions.question: What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam?

parts.text: List three mechanisms.

parts_raw.text: 22. What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam? (3)

questions.model_answer: (1) AmpC cephalosporinase / ESBL production (ceftolozane is stable to these and tazobactam inhibits many ESBLs). (2) Upregulation of RND efflux systems (MexAB-OprM, MexXY-OprM). (3) Loss of the OprD porin channel. These do not appreciably affect ceftolozane-tazobactam owing to its high PBP affinity; it is NOT active against metallo-β-lactamases (VIM, IMP, NDM) or class A KPC carbapenemases.

cohort_answer.text: Not affected by ESBL or AmpC enzymes; not affected by active efflux (upregulation of MexXY, MexAB); not appreciably affected by porin channel loss of OprD (cannot overcome MBL; not active against class A KPC, contrary to ceftaz-avi)

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman develops Clostridioides difficile infection after being on ciprofloxacin for a month.
questions.question_raw: 60 yo lady with c diff after being on cipro for a month.

parts.text: What are two treatment options for her?
From macrolide, penicillin, cephalosporin, doxycycline, clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, pick which is lowest risk for C. difficile.
She returns with a second recurrence. Name two antibiotic regimens you would consider and two non-antibiotic therapies.

parts_raw.text: What are 2 treatment options for her?
Pick which are the lowest risk for C diff : macrolide, pen, ceph, doxy, clinda, fluoroquinolones
She now comes back with a second recurrence. Name 2 abx regimens you would consider and 2 non-abx therapies

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID × 10 days (preferred). (2) Vancomycin 125 mg PO QID × 10 days.
b) Doxycycline (tetracyclines carry the lowest C. difficile risk of the listed agents; penicillins are also comparatively low, whereas fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins and clindamycin are highest).
c) Antibiotic: (1) Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID × 10 days (or extended/pulsed fidaxomicin); (2) Vancomycin 125 mg PO QID with tapered-and-pulsed course, or standard vancomycin followed by rifaximin. Non-antibiotic: (1) Fecal microbiota transplantation; (2) Bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B monoclonal antibody) as adjunct.
questions.beyond_mandell: C. difficile is not covered in the Pseudomonas chapter; answer per IDSA/SHEA 2017 (2021 focused update) C. difficile guidelines.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID × 10 days; (2) Vancomycin 125 mg PO QID × 10 days.
b) Antimicrobial: (1) Vancomycin 125 mg PO QID as a tapered-and-pulsed regimen (or vancomycin then rifaximin); (2) Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID × 10 days (or extended/pulsed dosing). Non-antimicrobial: (1) Fecal microbiota transplantation; (2) Bezlotoxumab.
c) Cephalosporin, quinolone (fluoroquinolone), clindamycin.

cohort_answer.text: First episode: Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days; Fidaxomicin 200mg PO BID x10 days. Recurrence: Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10-14 days with taper and pulse dosing (multiple potential regimens); Fidaxomicin 200mg PO BID x10 days; Fecal transplant; Monoclonal antibody therapy (bezlotoxumab). Most likely causative agents: Cephalosporin, quinolone, clindamycin

questions.question: A toxigenic strain of Clostridioides difficile is confirmed in each of the following scenarios; give the treatment regimen.
questions.question_raw: 25. C diff toxigenic strain confirmed in these 4 scenarios, what is the treatment regimen.

parts.text: 8-month-old infant.
Adult with first episode, non-severe.
Child with first episode, non-severe.
Adult with fulminant colitis.
Child with second recurrence.

parts_raw.text: 8 month old
adult with first episode, non-severe
child with first episode, non-severe
adult with fulminant colitis
child with 2nd recurrence

questions.model_answer:
a) 8-month-old: C. difficile testing/treatment is generally not recommended in infants <12 months because asymptomatic toxigenic colonization is common and infants lack toxin receptors; provide supportive care and seek an alternative diagnosis. If disease is genuinely attributable, metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg PO/IV TID.
b) Adult, first episode non-severe: Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID × 10 days (preferred), or vancomycin 125 mg PO QID × 10 days.
c) Child, first episode non-severe: Metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg PO TID (max 500 mg) × 10 days OR vancomycin 10 mg/kg PO QID (max 125 mg) × 10 days.
d) Adult, fulminant colitis: Vancomycin 500 mg PO/NG QID PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h; add vancomycin retention enema (500 mg in 100 mL q6h) if ileus, with early surgical consultation.
e) Child, second recurrence: Vancomycin tapered-and-pulsed course OR fidaxomicin; consider fecal microbiota transplantation.
questions.beyond_mandell: Not in the Pseudomonas chapter; regimens per IDSA/SHEA 2017 pediatric/adult and 2021 focused-update C. difficile guidelines.

questions.question: Give the resistance mechanism(s) for the following isolates.
questions.question_raw: Resistance mechanisms for the following:

parts.text: Pseudomonas resistant to meropenem and imipenem but susceptible to piperacillin and ceftazidime (give two).
Escherichia coli resistant to cefoxitin and ampicillin but intermediately susceptible to cefotaxime.

parts_raw.text: Pseudomonas R to mero and imi; sensitive to piperacillin and ceftaz (give two)
E coli R to cefoxitin, ampicillin but intermediately susceptible to CTX

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Loss/downregulation of the OprD porin, which admits carbapenems but not other β-lactams, giving carbapenem-selective resistance while sparing piperacillin/ceftazidime. (2) A carbapenem-hydrolyzing mechanism sparing penicillins/cephalosporins — e.g., OprD loss combined with RND efflux (MexAB-OprM removes meropenem) or a carbapenem-active enzyme.
b) AmpC-type β-lactamase (plasmid-mediated or derepressed chromosomal AmpC): confers cephamycin (cefoxitin) and ampicillin resistance, is not inhibited by clavulanate, and reduces oxyimino-cephalosporin (cefotaxime) susceptibility.
questions.beyond_mandell: The E. coli AmpC mechanism (part b) is not in the Pseudomonas chapter; per standard Enterobacterales resistance (Mandell antibacterial-resistance chapter / CLSI).

questions.question_raw: Question related to antibiotic resistance.

parts.text: Pseudomonas resistant to imipenem and meropenem but susceptible to piperacillin and ceftazidime. Name two mechanisms of resistance with molecule/gene as appropriate.
Escherichia coli resistant to cefoxitin, ampicillin and cefazolin but intermediate to ceftriaxone. Name one mechanism of resistance with molecule/gene as appropriate.

E coli with R to cefoxitin, amp and cefazolin but I to ceftriaxone. Name one mechanism of resistance with molecule/gene (as appropriate)

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Loss of the OprD porin (oprD mutation), producing carbapenem-selective resistance while sparing piperacillin and ceftazidime. (2) Upregulation of the MexAB-OprM RND efflux system (removes meropenem, not imipenem) and/or a carbapenemase (metallo-β-lactamase VIM/IMP/NDM) — name the gene if the profile fits OprD loss plus efflux for the carbapenem-only pattern.
b) AmpC cephalosporinase (e.g., plasmid-mediated CMY-2 or derepressed chromosomal ampC): resistance to cephamycins (cefoxitin), aminopenicillins and first-generation cephalosporins, clavulanate-non-inhibited, with reduced ceftriaxone susceptibility.
questions.beyond_mandell: The E. coli AmpC answer (part b) is outside the Pseudomonas chapter; per standard Enterobacterales resistance references.

questions.question: Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to imipenem and meropenem.

parts.text: Name two mechanisms of resistance.

parts_raw.text: Name two mechanisms of Pseudomonas resistance to IMI and MP?

questions.model_answer: (1) Loss/downregulation of the OprD porin (mutational), the principal cause of imipenem resistance and a contributor to meropenem resistance. (2) A carbapenemase — metallo-β-lactamase (VIM, IMP, NDM) or KPC — and/or upregulation of the MexAB-OprM efflux system (which removes meropenem but not imipenem); overexpressed AmpC can also contribute.

cohort_answer.text: MBL, carbapenemase; KPC, porins, efflux pump. Mutational loss of OprD porin, conferring resistance to imipenem; MBLs (VIM, IMP, SPM). Upregulation of the MexXY efflux system (a member of the RND family), which exports fluoroquinolones, tetracycline, aminoglycosides, and antipseudomonal β-lactam agents. Overexpression of AmpC chromosomal β-lactamases conferring resistance to multiple β-lactam antibiotics

questions.question: For each of the following isolates, name the mechanism of resistance: an Enterobacter species; a Pseudomonas resistant to imipenem/meropenem but susceptible to ceftazidime; a gram-negative bacillus resistant to meropenem but with an increased zone of inhibition when meropenem is combined with EDTA; an Escherichia coli resistant to cephalothin but susceptible to cefazolin.
questions.question_raw: Mechanism of Resistance

parts.text: For each of the following isolates, name the mechanism of resistance: Enterobacter; Pseudomonas resistant to imipenem/meropenem but susceptible to ceftazidime; a gram-negative bacillus resistant to meropenem but with an increased zone with meropenem plus EDTA; Escherichia coli resistant to cephalothin but susceptible to cefazolin.

parts_raw.text: For the following isolates, name the mechanism of resistance: Enterobacter; Pseudomonas R to Imi/Mero, S to Ceftaz; GNB R to mero but increased zone with mero + EDTA; E. coli R to cephalothin but S to cefazolin

questions.model_answer: (1) Enterobacter: inducible (or stably derepressed) chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase. (2) Pseudomonas R to imipenem/meropenem but S to ceftazidime: loss of the OprD porin plus efflux-pump upregulation (not carbapenemase-mediated). (3) GNB R to meropenem with larger zone on adding EDTA: metallo-beta-lactamase (EDTA chelates the active-site zinc, restoring activity). (4) E. coli R to cephalothin but S to cefazolin: a breakpoint/surrogate artefact - cephalothin is not a reliable predictor of susceptibility to cefazolin and other cephalosporins.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Enterobacter AmpC mechanism is in this chapter; porin/efflux, MBL-EDTA synergy, and the cephalothin surrogate issue are from CLSI resistance guidance (Mandell Ch. 18).

cohort_answer.text: Enterobacter - AmpC. Pseudomonas R to Imi/Mero, S to Ceftaz - Porin mediated and efflux pump. GNB R to mero but increased zone with mero+EDTA - Metallo beta lactamase. E. coli R to cephalothin but S to cefazolin - cephalothin breakpoints do not reliably predict susceptibilities of cephalexin and other cephalosporins.

questions.question: Ceftolozane-tazobactam.
questions.question_raw: Information on Ceftolozane/Tazobactam

parts.text: Name 3 mechanisms of resistance possessed by Pseudomonas aeruginosa that this antibiotic bypasses.

parts_raw.text: Name 3 mechanisms of resistance possessed by P. aeruginosa that this antibiotic bypasses

questions.model_answer: (1) Porin (OprD) loss/mutation — ceftolozane activity is unaffected by loss of the OprD outer-membrane porin. (2) Efflux pump activity — activity is unaffected by upregulated efflux systems. (3) AmpC β-lactamase — the large R2 pyrazole moiety particularly inhibits/withstands AmpC cephalosporinases, and tazobactam further inhibits class A and C enzymes.

cohort_answer.text: Efflux pumps (MexAB-OprD); Porin mutations (OprD); Modification of PBPs (ceftolozane potent inhibitor of PBP1b and 3); overexpression of AmpC (affinity for PBP4 not significant enough to induce AmpC); Class A and C beta-lactamases (tazobactam inhibits). Not effective against MBL, KPC, or OXA-48 carbapenemases

questions.question: A 43-year-old woman from Peru presents with gram-negative sepsis and a rapidly expanding perianal rash.
questions.question_raw: Q61 (2016 PM). 43F from Peru with GN sepsis, rapidly expanding perianal rash.

parts.text: What is the cause of the peri-anal rash?
What are three diagnostic tests to confirm the cause of the rash?
What are two infections that increase the likelihood of severe illness?
What are two non-infectious causes that increase the likelihood of severe disease?

parts_raw.text: A) What is the cause of the peri-anal rash?
B) What are 3 diagnostic tests to confirm the cause of the rash?
C) What are 2 infections that increase likelihood of severe illness?
D) What are 2 non-infectious causes that increase likelihood of severe disease?

questions.model_answer:
a) Larva currens — the migratory serpiginous rash of Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection/disseminated strongyloidiasis (with accompanying gram-negative sepsis from enteric bacterial translocation).
b) (1) Strongyloides serology (IgG ELISA); (2) Stool examination for larvae (repeated O&P, agar-plate culture or Baermann concentration; sputum/duodenal aspirate in hyperinfection); (3) Skin biopsy of the lesion for histopathology showing migrating larvae.
c) (1) HTLV-1 infection; (2) HIV/AIDS.
d) (1) Corticosteroid/immunosuppressive therapy; (2) Hematologic malignancy (also solid-organ transplant or severe malnutrition).
questions.beyond_mandell: Strongyloidiasis is not in the Pseudomonas chapter; per Mandell Strongyloides chapter and standard strongyloidiasis references.

cohort_answer.text: A) Larva currens caused by Strongyloidiasis infection. B) Strongyloides serology; Stool O+P (and possibly urine O+P); biopsy of skin lesion for histopathology. C) HTLV-1; HIV (has been reported in AIDS but not to extent expected, not AIDS-defining); any condition requiring steroid therapy associated with hyperinfection. D) Corticosteroid use; severe malnutrition; hematological malignancies; SOT.

questions.question: Ceftolozane-tazobactam and multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

parts.text: Name three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that would still render the isolate susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam.

parts_raw.text: Name three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that would still render the isolate susceptible to ceftolazane/tazobactam.

questions.model_answer: (1) Loss of the OprD porin channel. (2) Upregulation of RND efflux pumps (MexAB-OprM, MexXY-OprM). (3) AmpC cephalosporinase (and many ESBLs, inhibited by tazobactam). Ceftolozane's high PBP affinity and stability leave it active against these, so >80% of ceftazidime/meropenem-resistant isolates stay susceptible; it does NOT overcome metallo-β-lactamases or KPC.

questions.model_answer: a) Per the 2023 IDSA guidance for difficult-to-treat-resistance (DTR) Pseudomonas aeruginosa: (1) ceftolozane-tazobactam (2) ceftazidime-avibactam (3) imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam (4) cefiderocol. b) Cefiderocol - as a siderophore cephalosporin it is stable to serine- and metallo-beta-lactamases (VIM, IMP, NDM), so it is the option that retains activity in the presence of a metallo-beta-lactamase (ceftazidime-avibactam and imipenem-relebactam are NOT active against MBLs).
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell 9e names only ceftolozane-tazobactam and ceftazidime-avibactam and predates cefiderocol/imipenem-relebactam and the 2023 IDSA AMR gram-negative guidance, which is the source for the DTR-Pseudomonas agent list and cefiderocol's MBL activity.

questions.question: Antimicrobial mechanism of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Name three mechanisms of resistance that would still render the isolate susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam.
questions.question_raw: Q35 (2016 PM). Antimicrobial Mechanism of Resistance. a) Name 3 mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that would still render the isolate susceptible to Ceftolozane/Tazobactam

parts.text: Name three mechanisms that would still leave the isolate susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam.

parts_raw.text: Name 3 mechanisms that would still leave isolate susceptible to Ceftolozane/Tazobactam

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Loss/mutation of the OprD porin channel (confers carbapenem resistance but does not affect ceftolozane-tazobactam, which is unaffected by loss of porin channels). (2) Upregulation of the MexAB-OprM efflux system (meropenem resistance) - ceftolozane-tazobactam is unaffected by efflux pump upregulation. (3) Upregulation of the MexXY-OprM efflux system (aminoglycoside/cefepime resistance) - likewise does not compromise ceftolozane-tazobactam.

cohort_answer.text: Loss of OprD porin channel (typically carbapenem resistance); AmpC hyperproduction (chromosomal beta-lactamases); efflux pump (that pumps out other antibiotics but not ceftolozane/tazobactam); MexXY efflux system (exports fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, anti-pseudomonal beta-lactams); aminoglycoside modifying enzyme; parC/gyrA mutations; OXA-48 beta-lactamases.

questions.question: State the mechanism of resistance in each of the following scenarios.
questions.question_raw: Q37 (2014). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. What is the mechanism of resistance in the following scenarios: Serratia (Ertapenem R, Imipenem R, Meropenem R, CFTx S); Pseudomonas (Meropenem R, Imipenem S); E. gallinarum (Vancomycin R); E. cloacae (Cefepime S, Meropenem S, Ceftazidime R, Ertapenem R); MRSA (Daptomycin R); MRSA (Linezolid R)

parts.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each scenario: Serratia (Ertapenem R, Imipenem R, Meropenem R, Ceftriaxone S); Pseudomonas (Meropenem R, Imipenem S); Enterococcus gallinarum (Vancomycin R); Enterobacter cloacae (Cefepime S, Meropenem S, Ceftazidime R, Ertapenem R); MRSA (Daptomycin R); MRSA (Linezolid R).

parts_raw.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each scenario

questions.model_answer: (1) Serratia (carbapenems R, ceftriaxone S): Class A serine carbapenemase - Serratia marcescens enzyme (SME) (chromosomal blaSME); spares cephalosporins. (2) Pseudomonas (Meropenem R, Imipenem S): up-regulated efflux (MexAB-OprM), a meropenem substrate that does not affect imipenem. (3) E. gallinarum (Vancomycin R): intrinsic chromosomal vanC (D-Ala-D-Ser terminus), low-level resistance. (4) E. cloacae (Ceftaz R, Erta R, Cefepime/Mero S): derepressed AmpC (ceftazidime R, cefepime stable) combined with porin (OmpC/OmpF) loss producing ertapenem resistance while meropenem remains active. (5) MRSA (Daptomycin R): mprF mutation increasing membrane positive charge (reduced daptomycin binding). (6) MRSA (Linezolid R): 23S rRNA mutation (G2576T) at the domain V ribosomal target (or cfr methyltransferase).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the E. cloacae AmpC element is grounded in this chapter (p. 2682); SME, Pseudomonas efflux, vanC, and the MRSA mechanisms are established knowledge from Mandell resistance chapters.

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Serratia marcescens enzyme (SME) - carbapenemase Class A. Pseudomonas: MexAB-OprM efflux cassette. E. gallinarum: VanC gene presence (chromosomal). E. cloacae: intrinsic resistance to inducible AmpC (R to beta-lactams); OXA-48 (R to Erta, S to Mero with additional efflux pump or porin). MRSA Daptomycin R: mprF gene (phosphatidylglycerol lysyltransferase). MRSA Linezolid R: 23S RNA G2576T point mutation.

questions.question: State the resistance mechanism for each of the following scenarios.
questions.question_raw: Q43 (2012 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Enterobacter (unspecified); Pseudomonas - Imi/Mero (R), Ceftaz (S); GNB - Mero (R), increased zone with Mero+EDTA; E coli - Cephalothin (R), Cefazolin (S)

parts.text: State the resistance mechanism for each scenario: Enterobacter (unspecified profile); Pseudomonas (Imipenem R, Meropenem R, Ceftazidime S); gram-negative bacillus (Meropenem R, with increased inhibition zone when Meropenem is combined with EDTA); Escherichia coli (Cephalothin R, Cefazolin S).

parts_raw.text: State the resistance mechanism for each scenario

questions.model_answer: (1) Enterobacter: inducible chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase (risk of stable derepression). (2) Pseudomonas (Imi/Mero R, Ceftaz S): loss of the OprD porin channel (± efflux up-regulation affecting meropenem); cephalosporins unaffected because they do not require OprD. (3) GNB (Mero R, zone increased with Mero + EDTA): metallo-beta-lactamase (EDTA/zinc chelation restores activity - positive MBL synergy test). (4) E. coli (Cephalothin R, Cefazolin S): production of a narrow-spectrum plasmid-mediated beta-lactamase (penicillinase, e.g., SHV-1/TEM-1) hydrolyzing the more labile first-generation cephalosporin.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Enterobacter inducible AmpC is grounded in this chapter (p. 2682); the Pseudomonas OprD, MBL/EDTA, and E. coli penicillinase mechanisms are from Mandell resistance chapters.

cohort_answer.text: Enterobacter - AmpC. Pseudomonas (Imi/Mero R, Ceftaz S) - loss of OprD (porin mutation). GNB (Mero R, increased zone with Mero+EDTA) - metallo-beta-lactamase. E coli (Cephalothin R, Cefazolin S) - beta-lactamase (likely SHV).

questions.question: Antibacterial mechanisms of resistance. State the mechanism of resistance for each organism/antibiotic pair: Klebsiella pneumoniae to meropenem; Pseudomonas aeruginosa to meropenem; Enterococcus faecium to penicillin; Enterococcus faecalis with high-level aminoglycoside resistance; Streptococcus pneumoniae to moxifloxacin; Streptococcus pyogenes to erythromycin.
questions.question_raw: Q46 (2010 AM, 2009 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance (fill in the blank table): K. pneumoniae with Meropenem; P. aeruginosa with Meropenem; E faecium with penicillin; E faecalis with high level aminoglycoside resistance; S. pneumoniae with moxifloxacin; S. pyogenes with erythromycin

parts.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each organism/antibiotic pair.

parts_raw.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each organism/antibiotic pair

questions.model_answer:
(1) K. pneumoniae/meropenem: carbapenemase production - Ambler class A KPC (most common), class B metallo-beta-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP), class D OXA-48-type; also ESBL/AmpC plus porin loss (OmpK35/OmpK36).
(2) P. aeruginosa/meropenem: loss/downregulation of the OprD porin (with basal AmpC); acquired metallo-beta-lactamases (VIM, IMP); upregulated MexAB-OprM efflux (affects mero/dori but not imipenem).
(3) E. faecium/penicillin: overproduction of a low-affinity penicillin-binding protein PBP5 (altered target).
(4) E. faecalis/high-level aminoglycoside resistance: acquired aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme, classically the bifunctional AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia.
(5) S. pneumoniae/moxifloxacin: stepwise target mutations in the quinolone-resistance-determining regions of gyrA (DNA gyrase) and parC (topoisomerase IV).
(6) S. pyogenes/erythromycin: ribosomal methylation of 23S rRNA by an erm-encoded methylase (MLSB phenotype), or macrolide efflux via mef.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mechanisms are from Mandell Ch. 18 (antimicrobial resistance) / standard microbiology, not this Enterobacteriaceae chapter.

cohort_answer.text: K. pneumoniae/Meropenem: Ambler class D oxacillinases (OXAs); acquired class B beta-lactamases (VIM, NDM); Ambler Class A KPCs; reduced expression of OmpK35/OmpK36. P. aeruginosa/Meropenem: downregulated/absent OprD porin with background AmpC; MBLs (VIM, IMP, SPM-1 less common); upregulation of MexA-MexB-OprM efflux (resistant to mero/doripenem but not imipenem). E. faecium/Penicillin: altered PBPs (resistant pbp5 allele). E. faecalis/HLAR: bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-IE-APH(2'')-Ia. S. pneumoniae/Moxifloxacin: dual mutations in GyrA and ParC. S. pyogenes/Erythromycin: erm gene (ribosome methylation) - methylase enzymes dimethylate adenine on 23S rRNA of 50S subunit, disrupting MLS binding.

questions.question: Antibacterial mechanism of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
questions.question_raw: Q48 (2011 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Pseudomonas mechanisms of resistance.

parts.text: The isolate is resistant to imipenem and meropenem. What are two mechanisms of resistance?
The isolate is susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam and ceftazidime. What mechanism explains this pattern?

parts_raw.text: A) Isolate is Resistant to Imi and Mero. What are 2 mechanisms of resistance?
B) The isolate is susceptible to PipTazo and Ceftaz (?)

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Loss of the OprD porin channel - reduces carbapenem entry (predominantly imipenem). (2) An acquired carbapenemase (e.g., VIM/IMP/NDM metallo-beta-lactamase or KPC), OR upregulation of the MexAB-OprM efflux system, which additionally confers meropenem resistance - accounting for resistance to both carbapenems. b) Isolated loss of the OprD porin channel: OprD admits carbapenems but not other beta-lactams, so its loss confers carbapenem resistance while sparing piperacillin-tazobactam and ceftazidime, which retain susceptibility.

cohort_answer.text: A) Porin loss (OprD); upregulated efflux pump (MexXY); less commonly acquired carbapenemase. Common P. aeruginosa mechanisms: derepression of AmpC chromosomal beta-lactamases; mutational loss of OprD (Imi>Mero); MexA/MexB (Mero>Imi); upregulation of MexXY efflux system (exports FQ, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, anti-pseudomonal beta-lactams). B) Porin loss OprD; efflux pumps MexXY-OprM.

questions.question: Antibacterial mechanisms of resistance. Name the resistance mechanism(s) involved in each scenario: (a) Enterobacter - ceftazidime resistant, cefotaxime resistant, piperacillin-tazobactam resistant, imipenem susceptible; (b) Escherichia coli - ampicillin resistant, cefazolin susceptible, cephalothin intermediate; (c) Pseudomonas - imipenem/meropenem resistant, piperacillin-tazobactam/ceftazidime susceptible; (d) Pseudomonas - imipenem resistant MIC=64, imipenem MIC with EDTA in agar=0.5.
questions.question_raw: Q49 (2008). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Name the resistance mechanism(s) involved: a) Enterobacter - CTZ (R), CTX (R), PipTazo (R), Imipenem (S); b) E coli - Amp (R), Cefazolin (S), Cephalothin (I); c) Pseudomonas - Imi/Mero (R), PipTazo/CTZ (S); d) Pseudomonas - Imipenem (R) MIC=64, MIC with EDTA in agar=0.5

parts.text: State the resistance mechanism for each scenario.

parts_raw.text: State the resistance mechanism for each scenario

questions.model_answer:
a) Derepression (stable hyperproduction) of the inducible chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase (Ambler class C); carbapenem-sparing because AmpC does not hydrolyze imipenem.
b) Broad-spectrum penicillinase (Ambler class A, e.g., TEM-1/SHV-1) - hydrolyzes ampicillin but not cefazolin.
c) Selective carbapenem resistance with retained anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam activity indicates loss/downregulation of the OprD porin (with basal AmpC); an efflux component may coexist.
d) Metallo-beta-lactamase (Ambler class B) - the dramatic fall in imipenem MIC in the presence of the zinc chelator EDTA is diagnostic of a zinc-dependent carbapenemase.
questions.beyond_mandell: Enterobacter chromosomal AmpC derepression is described in this chapter (p. 2682); the Pseudomonas porin-loss and metallo-beta-lactamase mechanisms are from Ch. 18/standard microbiology.

cohort_answer.text: a) De-repression of chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase (class C) in presence of beta-lactams. b) SHV beta-lactamase (class A). c) OprD porin loss (efflux pump would also likely render resistant to tazo/ceftaz). d) Metallo-beta-lactamase (class B).

questions.question: Antibacterial mechanisms of resistance: state the resistance mechanism and suggested treatment for each of macrolides (and explain the D test), beta-lactamases, and Pseudomonas with carbapenems.
questions.question_raw: Q53 (2007). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Name the resistance mechanism for each, as well as suggested treatment: Macrolides (+ explain D test); Beta-lactamases; Pseudomonas and carbapenems

parts.text: State the mechanisms and treatments for each category (macrolides with the D test, beta-lactamases, and Pseudomonas with carbapenems).

parts_raw.text: State mechanisms and treatments for each category

questions.model_answer: a) Macrolides: (mechanisms) efflux via mef genes (low-level, MIC <=16) and ribosomal methylation via erm genes (high-level, MIC >=64). D test: an erythromycin disk placed near a clindamycin disk; blunting/flattening of the clindamycin zone on the side facing erythromycin (D-shaped zone) indicates inducible erm-mediated clindamycin resistance, so clindamycin should not be used. Treatment: beta-lactam or vancomycin for susceptible gram-positive cocci. Beta-lactamases: enzymatic hydrolysis of the beta-lactam ring (penicillinases, ESBLs, AmpC cephalosporinases, carbapenemases); treat by adding a beta-lactamase inhibitor, using a stable agent (carbapenem for ESBL), or switching classes for carbapenemase producers. Pseudomonas and carbapenems: (1) loss of OprD porin (chiefly imipenem), (2) upregulated efflux (MexAB-OprM, chiefly meropenem), and (3) acquired carbapenemases (metallo-beta-lactamases VIM/IMP/NDM, KPC, GES); treat per susceptibilities with an alternative active agent (e.g., ceftolozane-tazobactam or ceftazidime-avibactam for non-MBL producers).
questions.beyond_mandell: Macrolide resistance mechanisms (mef/erm) and the D test are not covered in this Pseudomonas chapter; that content rests on general antimicrobial-resistance knowledge (Mandell resistance chapters/CLSI).

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides: efflux (mefA gene, lower level resistance MIC<=16); ribosomal methylation (ermB gene, high level MIC>=64). D test checks for inducible clindamycin resistance via inducible erm gene - blunting of zone of inhibition around clindamycin proximal to erythromycin disk (D-shaped zone = positive, indicates induced clindamycin resistance); suggested treatment: beta-lactam or vancomycin for GPC, septra for MRSA. Beta-lactamases: bacteria produce enzymes breaking down beta-lactam (penicillinase, cephalosporinase/ESBL, carbapenemase); treatment depends on spectrum - use cephalosporin/aztreonam/carbapenem, add beta-lactamase inhibitor, or switch classes (tigecycline, colistin). Pseudomonas and carbapenems: porin loss (OprD deficiency confers high resistance esp to imipenem); efflux pump; carbapenemase.

questions.question: List and describe three mechanisms by which Pseudomonas aeruginosa is resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics, giving an example of an antibiotic affected by each, and also address aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and multidrug resistance.
questions.question_raw: Q56 (2004). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. List and describe 3 mechanisms by which P. aeruginosa are resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics. Give an example of an antibiotic affected by each. Also cover Aminoglycosides, Fluoroquinolones, MDR

parts.text: Describe the resistance mechanisms with examples for beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and multidrug resistance.

parts_raw.text: Describe resistance mechanisms with examples for beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and MDR

questions.model_answer: a) Beta-lactams (3 mechanisms): (1) Enzymatic inactivation - AmpC chromosomal cephalosporinase confers resistance to all beta-lactams except fourth-generation cephalosporins/carbapenems unless overproduced; example: ceftazidime. (2) Efflux pumps - MexAB-OprM removes meropenem (not imipenem), MexXY-OprM removes cefepime (not ceftazidime); example: meropenem/cefepime. (3) Decreased outer-membrane permeability - loss of the OprD porin; example: carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem). Aminoglycosides: aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (e.g., nucleotidyltransferase (2')-I -> gentamicin/tobramycin; acetyltransferase (6')-II -> netilmicin), efflux via MexXY-OprM, and reduced membrane uptake; example: gentamicin. Fluoroquinolones: multidrug RND efflux pumps (MexAB-OprM, MexXY-OprM) and target-enzyme mutations (DNA gyrase/topoisomerase); example: ciprofloxacin. MDR: MexAB-OprM and MexXY-OprM RND efflux systems confer intrinsic multidrug resistance across fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, beta-lactams, tetracyclines, tigecycline, and chloramphenicol.
questions.beyond_mandell: Fluoroquinolone target-enzyme (gyrA/parC) mutations are established knowledge; the chapter emphasizes efflux for fluoroquinolone resistance.

cohort_answer.text: Beta-lactams: Enzymatic inhibition (AmpC cephalosporinases - Ceftazidime; ESBL); Upregulation of efflux pumps (MexAB-OprM - resistance to Meropenem but S to imipenem; MexXY-OprM - resistant to Cefepime but S to Ceftazidime); Decreased outer membrane porin expression (loss of OprD channel - Meropenem, Imipenem). Aminoglycosides: Enzymatic inhibition (AAC6, ANT2); Efflux (MexXY); Ribosomal methylation. Fluoroquinolones: Multidrug efflux pumps (MexAB-OprM, MexCD-OprJ, MexEF-OprN); alteration of target enzymes (DNA gyrase gyrA mutations, topoisomerase parC). MDR: MexAB-OprM and MexXY-OprM efflux systems (RND family) confer intrinsic multidrug resistance to fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, beta-lactams, tetracyclines, tigecycline, chloramphenicol.

parts.text: What are two distinct skin manifestations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa?

parts_raw.text: A) What are 2 distinct skin manifestations of P. aeruginosa?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Ecthyma gangrenosum - characteristic of P. aeruginosa bacteremia in neutropenic/immunocompromised hosts (red macules progressing to bullae, then a gray-black necrotic eschar with surrounding erythema). questions.question: Identify the mechanism of resistance. A Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate is resistant to carbapenems but susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam. An Escherichia coli isolate is resistant to cefoxitin but susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam, carbapenems, and ceftazidime.

parts.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to carbapenems, susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam - what is the mechanism?
Escherichia coli resistant to cefoxitin, susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam, carbapenem, and ceftazidime - what is the mechanism?

parts_raw.text: Pseudomonas R carbapenems, S PTZ - mechanism?
E coli R cefoxitin, S PTZ, S carbapenem, S ceftazidime - mechanism?

questions.model_answer: a) Loss/mutation of the OprD porin channel: OprD admits carbapenems but not other beta-lactams, so its loss produces carbapenem resistance while sparing piperacillin-tazobactam. b) An AmpC-type cephalosporinase: resistance to cefoxitin (a cephamycin, not protected by tazobactam) is the hallmark of AmpC, while the low expression here leaves piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, and carbapenems active.
questions.beyond_mandell: The E. coli AmpC interpretation is established Enterobacterales resistance knowledge; this chapter covers Pseudomonas, not E. coli.

cohort_answer.text: Pseudomonas: OprD porin mutation (does not cause Piptazo resistance). E. coli: unclear/possibly misremembered stem; discussion suggests possible TEM-1/SHV-1 or AmpC, though the given susceptibility pattern is inconsistent with classic AmpC or ESBL patterns.

questions.question: What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam?
questions.question_raw: 22. What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam? (3)

parts.text: What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam?

parts_raw.text: What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam? (3)

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Loss/mutation of the OprD porin channel - ceftolozane-tazobactam is unaffected by loss of porin channels. (2) Upregulation of the MexAB-OprM efflux system - ceftolozane-tazobactam is unaffected by efflux pump upregulation. (3) Upregulation of the MexXY-OprM efflux system - likewise does not compromise ceftolozane-tazobactam. (Over 80% of ceftazidime- or meropenem-resistant isolates remain susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam.)

cohort_answer.text: Unaffected by porin channels (Mandell); unaffected by upregulation of efflux pumps (Mandell); MexXY efflux system (exports fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, and anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam agents); Enzymes: TEM-1, SHV-1, CTX-M, AmpC or ESBL (chromosomal beta lactamases); Aminoglycoside modifying enzymes (reduce susceptibility to all AG).

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Species level: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ecthyma gangrenosum is its characteristic manifestation of bacteremia in neutropenic hosts). (2) Genus level: Aspergillus species (ecthyma-like lesions can also be caused by other gram-negatives, fungi such as Aspergillus/Fusarium, and viruses). b) Empiric broad-spectrum antipseudomonal beta-lactam - piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, or meropenem - as monotherapy per febrile-neutropenia guidance; add a second antipseudomonal agent (aminoglycoside or antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone) if critically ill or high local resistance, and add vancomycin if hemodynamically unstable or MRSA/skin involvement, with treatment of the bacteremia and local wound care.
questions.beyond_mandell: The empiric febrile-neutropenia regimen (monotherapy plus escalation criteria, addition of vancomycin) derives from IDSA febrile-neutropenia guidance rather than this chapter, which describes antipseudomonal therapy generally.

cohort_answer.text: A) Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staph aureus, Strep pyogenes; fungal: Candida albicans, Mucor, Aspergillus, Fusarium. B) PipTazo (antipseudomonal) or Meropenem; double cover with aminoglycoside if critically ill; add anti-MRSA agent (Vanco) if critically ill.

parts_raw.text: 2 causes of infectious dermatitis from hot tub exposure?
1 (or 2) causes of pneumonia from hot tub exposure
Most common parasitic cause of widespread waterborne diarrheal illness?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Pseudomonas aeruginosa hot tub folliculitis (also hot hand-foot syndrome/green nail syndrome). (2) Nontuberculous mycobacteria (Mycobacterium avium complex). b) (1) Mycobacterium avium complex hypersensitivity pneumonitis ('hot tub lung'). (2) Legionella pneumophila. c) Cryptosporidium species - the most frequent pathogen implicated in recreational-water outbreaks and a leading parasitic cause of waterborne diarrhea (Giardia is the other principal cause).
questions.beyond_mandell: Hot tub lung (MAC hypersensitivity pneumonitis), Legionella, and nontuberculous mycobacterial dermatitis are not in this Pseudomonas chapter; that content rests on general/PHAC-CDC waterborne-disease knowledge.
questions.cohort_conflict: The chapter identifies Cryptosporidium as the most frequent recreational-water pathogen, so for waterborne illness Cryptosporidium is favored over the cohort's Giardia.

cohort_answer.text: Dermatitis: Hot tub folliculitis (Pseudomonas aeruginosa) - painful pruritic pustules within 24-48h, self-resolves 7-14d; Hot foot syndrome (Pseudomonas) - painful red nodular lesions on soles, self-limiting 7-10d; Green nail syndrome (pseudomonas) with onychomycosis; Mycobacterium species. Pneumonia: MAC hypersensitivity pneumonitis ('hot tub lung'), usually self-limiting, may need prednisone +/- antimycobacterial; Legionellosis (usually L. pneumophila). Parasite: Giardia lamblia (most common cause of parasitic diarrhea worldwide; cryptosporidium also very high incidence); tx metronidazole/tinidazole/nitazoxanide, paromomycin if pregnant first trimester
